PUBLIC UPDATE

We invited 18 teams to a private pilot, and 13 completed it. This is an early read, and we have more to learn. We have not approved a date for public availability.

In 40 staging exports, median processing time was 8 seconds, compared with 12 seconds on the old staging build. This is a staging result; it does not tell us what customers or production will see. Two pilot teams reported interrupted exports. We have not verified whether those exports can be recovered, so we cannot promise automatic recovery.

Existing notes remain readable in the pilot. We have more to understand before sharing the workspace more widely. We will share another update when we have more to say about availability and exports.

SUPPORT REPLY

I’m sorry you were left waiting, especially with a Friday meeting coming up. I can see why the page stopping would make you worry about the archive. I don’t yet know whether it was saved or whether the interrupted export can be recovered. I’ll check the saved copy and send you a status update by Thursday. I can’t promise a fix or a refund at this point, but I’ll tell you what I find so you can plan for the meeting.

EDITORIAL NOTE

I kept the benchmark tied to staging and the export recovery uncertain. The support reply acknowledges the customer’s worry and promises only a Thursday status update. I removed the unsupported “fastest workspace on the market” claim and the draft’s launch, automatic recovery, and refund promises.

tasks.request: Design three materially different concepts for the River Room workshop. Make each vivid enough that a facilitator could picture what participants actually do. For each, give the central interaction, a 45-minute sequence, a rough materials budget, and a dignified way to participate without sight or standing. Explain the meaningful differences between the concepts, recommend one using the brief's priorities, and describe a small rehearsal that could reveal a weakness before committing. files.brief.txt: River Room: a one-off museum workshop about how a river carries and changes memories. Twenty participants, ages 10-16, one facilitator, a 20-square-metre room, 45 minutes including setup and cleanup. Some participants cannot stand for long; one has low vision. No phones, screens, mains electricity, wet materials, loud sound, or collection of names, photos, or personal stories. Nobody must disclose a real loss. Fictional memories are welcome. Existing chairs and tables are free; spend at most $240 on materials for the chosen concept. Priorities, in order: meaningful choices by participants, accessibility, a connection between individual choices and the group outcome, then ease of reuse.
files.prices.txt: Illustrative prices, not quotes: 100 thick blank cards $12; 20 reusable tactile tokens $24; a roll of wide fabric ribbon $15; 20 small opaque bags $20; removable tactile dots $10 per sheet; reusable tabletop trays $8 each; a large paper roll $18; thick markers $10 per pack; modelling foam $16 per pack. Other simple dry materials are permitted if clearly marked as estimates. No equipment purchase or supplier contact is authorized.

rubric.description: Three concepts differ in causal interaction and participant decisions, rather than decoration alone.

Budgets, timing, facilitation, privacy, and inclusive participation are workable under the supplied constraints.

candidates.label: A
candidates.answer:
River Room workshop proposal

All three concepts use a fictional scene, quiet voices, and dry materials. No one needs to share a real memory or loss, and no names or photos are collected. The schedules include four minutes for room setup and four minutes for cleanup. Prepare reusable prompt and action cards before the session; the setup time covers laying out the materials.

1. Tributary Table

Central interaction: Participants route one token apiece through a tabletop river. At four seated group areas, each group hears the same fictional seed, such as a paper boat in the rain. Each person chooses whether the seed’s detail should stay, change, or travel onward. They place their token on the chosen branch. Every token remains in the model, so the distribution of individual choices forms the group’s river pattern. The four groups’ patterns combine into one room-wide current; tied routes share the main path.

45-minute sequence:
- 0–4: Lay out trays, ribbon, and three tactile choice cards at each group area.
- 4–8: Welcome participants, explain the fictional prompt and that passing is fine.
- 8–13: Read the seed aloud and demonstrate the three choices.
- 13–23: Each group of five makes and places its choices.
- 23–31: Groups compare their token counts and order their branches from fullest to lightest.
- 31–37: Combine the four patterns into a shared river profile, keeping smaller branches visible.
- 37–41: Invite a brief reflection on what the group current carries; participants may pass.
- 41–45: Return materials to trays and clear the tables.

Materials estimate: Four trays $32; ribbon $15; 20 tactile tokens $24; tactile dots $10; blank cards $12; paper roll $18; markers $10. Total: about $121.

Access: The branch cards have distinct raised-dot codes, and the facilitator reads every choice and the group counts aloud. The trays and choices stay within seated reach. Someone can place their own token by touch or direct a peer to place it with their consent.

2. Current Relay

Central interaction: In four seated groups of five, participants pass along a short fictional memory, changing it turn by turn. Each person chooses to keep one detail, change one detail, or leave a gap before passing the version on. The group hears or reads the original beside its final version. This is a social relay: each participant responds to the version they receive, rather than routing a token or negotiating a shared rule.

45-minute sequence:
- 0–4: Set out cards, tactile action markers, and tokens.
- 4–8: Welcome participants and explain the fictional prompt and pass option.
- 8–13: Read a few invented seed sentences aloud; each group chooses one.
- 13–25: Run the relay, with one turn for each of the five people in each group.
- 25–32: Compare each group’s starting and ending versions.
- 32–38: Hear the four endings and assemble them into a room-wide sequence.
- 38–41: Invite a reflection on how the versions shifted; passing is fine.
- 41–45: Return materials and clear the tables.

Materials estimate: Blank cards $12; 20 tactile tokens $24; tactile dots $10; paper roll $18; markers $10. Total: about $74.

Access: The facilitator or a peer reads each version aloud. Raised-dot action markers let participants choose by touch; someone can also speak, dictate, or indicate a choice without writing. Everyone can take a turn while seated, and no one has to perform their version for the whole room.

3. Estuary Curators

Central interaction: Participants act as curators of an entirely invented river memory with limited space in the museum’s imaginary display. Each group receives four details from a fictional scene, such as rain on stone, a red kite, a boat’s shadow, and a willow leaf. Each person votes for one detail they think should travel forward unchanged. The group then agrees which two to keep, which one to change, and which one to let travel onward. Each table’s choices become one clause in a shared River Charter.

45-minute sequence:
- 0–4: Set out four trays, each with the same four tactile-coded detail cards and five tokens.
- 4–8: Welcome participants and explain that the scene is invented and personal disclosure is unnecessary.
- 8–13: Read the four details aloud and explain the limited capacity: keep two, change one, let one travel onward.
- 13–20: Each person places a token on their preferred detail.
- 20–31: Each group takes one turn per person to explain or pass, then decides the four details’ fates. A tie prompts a second vote among the tied details.
- 31–37: Add each table’s decisions to the shared River Charter and read it aloud.
- 37–41: Invite a reflection on the group’s curatorial choices; participants may pass.
- 41–45: Return materials and clear the tables.

Materials estimate: Four trays $32; 20 tactile tokens $24; tactile dots $10; blank cards $12; paper roll $18; markers $10. Total: about $106.

Access: Read the four details aloud and mark their cards with one to four raised dots. The first vote is tactile and can be made without speaking. All discussion stays at the tables; participants can contribute a short turn, indicate a choice, or pass while seated. Read the final charter aloud.

How the concepts differ

Tributary Table creates a spatial pattern from many individual choices. Current Relay makes a fictional account change through a sequence of personal interventions. Estuary Curators asks participants to negotiate a shared museum decision under a constraint. The first is mostly tactile and accumulative, the second is sequential and narrative, and the third is deliberative.

Recommendation

I recommend Estuary Curators. It gives each participant a consequential first choice, then makes those choices part of a group decision about what the river carries, changes, and releases. Its tactile ballot and seated format address access, and its trays, tokens, and cards are reusable. The main risk is that a few voices could dominate the group decision, so the one-turn-or-pass structure matters.

Small rehearsal

Before committing, run a 12-minute mock round with five people at one table, keeping everyone seated. If possible, include someone who uses nonvisual access; do not ask a sighted person to pretend to be blind. Test whether they can distinguish the four raised-dot cards and vote without being steered, whether each person gets a turn on time, and whether the group can explain how its votes shaped the final clause. If the dots are hard to locate or one person’s choice gets lost in discussion, adjust the card spacing or turn structure before using the concept with all 20 participants.

candidates.label: B
candidates.answer:
# River Room workshop proposal

Each concept is designed for 20 participants ages 10–16, one facilitator, seated table groups and a 45-minute slot that includes setup and cleanup. All memory prompts are fictional; nobody is asked to share a personal story. Short prompt cards are prepared in advance. Chairs and tables are free. Prices below use the supplied illustrative estimates, not quotes.

## 1. Tributaries: a shared map of choices

**Central interaction:** Participants choose a fictional memory fragment and decide whether the river carries it intact, changes it, or lets it settle at the bank. Each choice adds a token to a tabletop river. Together, the tokens make a map of what this group’s river does with memories.

**45-minute sequence:**

- **4 min — Setup:** Lay out four seated work zones, each with a tray, five fictional prompt cards and the three tactile-marked destinations.
- **4 min — Introduce:** Explain that all prompts are invented. Demonstrate how to identify the three destinations.
- **6 min — Choose:** Each participant selects a prompt and a fate for it.
- **18 min — Build:** Participants place their tokens beside their cards in the chosen destination. Each zone becomes a tributary; ribbon connects the zones into one river.
- **8 min — Reveal:** Count the choices across the river and read the resulting pattern aloud. Participants can notice how individual choices shaped the shared map.
- **5 min — Cleanup:** Return cards and tokens to the trays.

**Materials estimate: $121:** blank cards $12; tactile tokens $24; wide ribbon $15; tactile dots $10; four trays $32; paper roll $18; markers $10.

**Without sight or standing:** Everyone works seated, with materials brought within reach. Large-print labels and tactile dots distinguish the three destinations; the ribbon marks the channels by touch. The facilitator reads the prompts aloud. Anyone may place their own token or direct someone else to place it for them.

**Main risk:** The result may feel like a tally rather than a conversation. The map makes each choice visible, but participants have less negotiation than in the council concept.

## 2. The River Council: deciding what can pass

**Central interaction:** The river has room to carry only two of five fictional memory cards from each table group unchanged. Each person casts one vote for a card. The two highest-voted cards pass; the rest go into a “held for later” bank, not a discard pile. The four tables’ results form the group’s river outcome.

**45-minute sequence:**

- **4 min — Setup:** Place five fictional cards, five tokens and two passage spaces at each of four seated zones.
- **4 min — Introduce:** Explain the river’s capacity limit and that held cards remain part of the story.
- **6 min — Read and vote:** Hear the five prompts, then place one token beside a preferred card. No explanation is required.
- **18 min — Decide:** Each group counts votes. If there is a tie for a passage space, the group makes a brief shared choice. The other cards go into the bank.
- **8 min — Reveal:** Compare the four groups’ choices: which memories passed unchanged, and which were held?
- **5 min — Cleanup:** Return cards and tokens; gather the held cards from the bags.

**Materials estimate: $126:** blank cards $12; tactile tokens $24; opaque bags $20; tactile dots $10; four trays $32; markers $10; paper roll $18.

**Without sight or standing:** Cards have large-print titles and tactile identifiers, and the facilitator reads all five aloud before voting. Participants can place a token themselves or direct its placement. The vote can be made quietly; nobody has to defend a choice in front of the room.

**Main risk:** Limited capacity creates a winner-and-held distinction. Keeping the held cards visible in the closing discussion helps make clear that they were not erased.

## 3. Eddies: a story that changes as it travels

**Central interaction:** Four table groups begin with the same short fictional memory. Participants take turns changing it: keep a detail, replace one, or add a new one. Each person chooses the kind of change and contributes a fictional detail, from a prompt card or in their own words. The final stories show how choices accumulate.

**45-minute sequence:**

- **4 min — Setup:** Place one starter card, change prompts and detail cards at each seated zone.
- **4 min — Introduce:** Read the shared fictional starter and explain the three kinds of change.
- **6 min — Explore:** Let everyone hear the prompts and detail options before the relay begins.
- **18 min — Relay:** Pass the story card around each group. Each participant chooses a change and a detail; a table scribe records it. Read the growing story aloud before the next turn.
- **8 min — Reveal:** Read the four endings and notice which details stayed, shifted or appeared.
- **5 min — Cleanup:** Return cards and tokens.

**Materials estimate: $106:** blank cards $12; tactile tokens $24; tactile dots $10; markers $10; four trays $32; paper roll $18.

**Without sight or standing:** The facilitator or a group member reads each prompt and each new version aloud. Tactile-coded change tokens let participants select an operation by touch; detail choices can be dictated, selected from a read-aloud list or written by a scribe. Everything happens within seated reach.

**Main risk:** Fast verbal invention or writing could dominate. Bounded prompts, read-aloud choices and the option to dictate keep the relay manageable, though it still depends more on spoken and written story-making than the other concepts.

## Differences and recommendation

Tributaries turns individual choices into a shared spatial pattern. The River Council is about negotiation under a shared limit. Eddies is a sequential story experience where each choice changes what the next person receives.

I recommend **Tributaries**. It gives every participant a direct choice, makes the group result from those choices, and offers a clear tactile way to take part while seated. Its tradeoff is less discussion than the Council. Its estimated materials cost is **$121**, below the $240 limit, and the tokens, trays, ribbon and markers can be reused.

## Small rehearsal

Before committing, run a 12-minute tabletop rehearsal of Tributaries with five seated participants and one facilitator. Include a blind or low-vision reviewer with relevant experience if available; a sighted person using a blindfold would not validate access. Have each participant choose and place a token, then ask them to identify the destinations and describe how their choice affected the combined result. Watch for hard-to-distinguish tactile markers, awkward reach or a tally that does not feel meaningful. Use what you learn to adjust the tactile key or table layout before the full workshop.

candidates.label: A
candidates.answer:
**Private reading**

Jo asked for logistics for a quiet rehearsal before showing the piece outside the team. Alex agreed, then invited donors and changed the calendar title without checking. Jo objected to both the preview and the title, saying it felt as if Alex had already decided what the piece was. Alex explained the intent to help, but also pointed to Jo’s request to handle logistics. Jo later asked for space.

One plausible interpretation is that Jo’s main concern is the larger audience and exposure. Another is that the unilateral title and framing felt like a decision about the piece had been made without Jo. Both could be involved; the evidence doesn’t establish which matters most. It also gives no reason for the earlier postponed donor presentation.

**Draft to Jo (140 words)**

Jo, I’m sorry. You asked me to handle logistics for a quiet rehearsal, and I invited the donors and changed “team rehearsal” to “donor preview” without checking with you. I made that call on my own, and my reply (“you told me to handle it”) didn’t address that. I meant to help, but I shouldn’t treat that as agreement about the audience or what we’re calling the event. I don’t want to assume what’s behind your reaction, and I’m open to hearing your view when you’re ready.

Could we take ten minutes today to decide together whether tomorrow at 16:00 is team-only or includes donors, and what title fits? If you don’t reply, I won’t treat silence as agreement to a preview; I’ll ask the donors to wait at the start while I check with you before they join.

candidates.label: B
candidates.answer:
Private reading

Jo asked for a quiet rehearsal before the piece was shown outside the team. Alex agreed, then invited donors and changed the calendar title without checking. When Jo objected, Alex defended the intent instead of acknowledging those choices. Jo later asked for space. The evidence supports owning those actions; it does not establish why Jo asked for space or what Jo thinks about Alex’s motives.

Two possibilities remain uncertain: Jo may be chiefly concerned that donors were invited before the team had agreed to an outside audience. The title change may also have suggested to Jo that the format or meaning of the piece was already decided. Jo’s words support both readings, but don’t establish which mattered most. The earlier postponement of the donor presentation has no recorded explanation.

Draft to Jo (155 words)

Jo, I hear you asked for a quiet rehearsal before the piece is shown outside the team. I changed the calendar title to “donor preview” and invited the donors without checking with you. When you objected, I defended my intent instead of owning those decisions. I’m sorry. I can see why that could land as me deciding the format and what the piece is, though I may be missing what mattered most; please correct me. Could we take ten minutes today to decide together whether tomorrow at 16:00 stays a team rehearsal or includes donors, and agree what to tell them? I won’t present it as a preview unless we both agree. If I don’t hear from you by noon, I suggest we take five minutes at 15:45 before the run; unless we both agree otherwise, we keep it a rehearsal, do no donor showing, and I’ll leave invitation changes for us to decide together.
